lessons.title: Types of Cattle Housing
lessons.body: In Africa, cattle housing ranges from simple overnight kraals to permanent barns, depending on climate, budget, and cattle purpose. For dry regions like the Sahel, a thorn-bush kraal (boma) made from acacia branches is cheap and effective. Build it circular, 10â15 m diameter for 20 cattle, with a 1.5 m high wall. For wetter areas, a raised wooden platform (0.5 m off ground) prevents mud and foot rot. In highlands like Kenya or Ethiopia, a simple three-sided shed with a corrugated iron roof works well; open side faces away from prevailing winds. For dairy cattle, a free-stall barn with individual cubicles (1.2 m wide x 2.5 m long per cow) is ideal, but expensive. A cheaper alternative is a loose housing system with a concrete floor and bedding area. In hot zones, use shade cloth or thatch roof (thatch is cooler than iron). Always include a holding pen and a crush for veterinary work. For calves, a separate hutch or pen with clean bedding is essential to prevent pneumonia. In all types, ensure good drainage: slope floor 2â3% toward a gutter. Local materials like bamboo, mud bricks, or palm fronds can reduce costs. Remember, housing protects against theft, predators, and extreme weather, but cattle still need daily exercise. A simple corral with a windbreak and shade is often enough for beef cattle in extensive systems.

lessons.title: Designing Barns and Sheds
lessons.body: Designing a cattle barn starts with the number of animals and their size. A mature cow needs about 4â5 mÂ² of resting space in a loose barn, plus 1.5 mÂ² for feeding and walking. For a 20-cow herd, a shed 10 m wide x 20 m long gives 200 mÂ², enough for resting and a feed alley. Orient the shed east-west so the long side faces north-south? Actually, in hot climates, orient the ridge east-west to minimize sun on the long walls; the roof overhang should be 1 m to block midday sun. Use a roof pitch of 15â20 degrees for iron sheets, or 30 degrees for thatch. Ventilation: leave a 0.5 m gap under the roof ridge (open ridge) to let hot air escape. Floor: concrete is best for hygiene, but expensive. A cheaper option is compacted murram (red soil) with a 10 cm layer of sand on top, replaced weekly. For dairy, include a milking parlour: a 4 m x 6 m area with a 1 m high concrete wall and a 0.9 m wide crush. Feed troughs: 0.6 m wide, 0.4 m deep, with a 0.5 m high lip to prevent spillage. Water troughs: 1 m long per 10 cows, with a float valve. For calves, build individual pens 1.5 m x 2 m with slatted wooden floors. Always include a 3 m wide access road for feed delivery. In flood-prone areas, raise the floor 0.5 m above ground. Use local timber for posts (e.g., eucalyptus) treated with used engine oil to deter termites. Roofing: corrugated iron is common but noisy; add a ceiling of sisal sacks for insulation.

lessons.title: Fencing and Handling Facilities
lessons.body: Fencing keeps cattle in, predators out, and controls grazing. For permanent boundary fences, use wooden posts (10 cm diameter, 2 m long, buried 0.6 m deep) every 3 m, with 4 strands of barbed wire at 30 cm, 60 cm, 90 cm, and 120 cm heights. In tsetse fly areas, use treated poles and wire. For rotational grazing, electric fencing is cheaper: a single strand of polywire at 60 cm height, powered by a 12V battery energizer (e.g., 5 km range). Train cattle to electric fences by baiting with hay. For handling, a basic crush (chute) is essential. Build a race 0.7 m wide, 3 m long, with a head gate at the end. Use 5 cm steel pipes or hardwood posts. A simple head gate can be made from two 1.5 m wooden levers. For dehorning, vaccination, and AI, a crush with a squeeze mechanism (two hinged sides) is safer. Add a loading ramp: 1.2 m wide, 3 m long, with 20 cm high cleats every 30 cm. For sorting, use a circular pen with a swinging gate. In East Africa, many farmers use a 'kraal' made of thorn branches for night enclosure; reinforce with wire mesh if theft is common. Always provide a footbath at the entrance: 2 m long, 0.2 m deep, filled with 5% copper sulphate solution to prevent foot rot. Check fences weekly for loose wires and replace rotten posts immediately. Remember, a good fence saves labour and prevents disease spread from neighbouring herds.

lessons.title: Water Systems and Supply
lessons.body: Cattle need 30â50 litres of clean water per day for drinking, plus more for cleaning. A lactating cow can drink up to 80 litres in hot weather. Plan for 50 litres per cow per day. Sources: borehole, river, dam, or rainwater harvesting. For a borehole, install a hand pump or solar pump. A solar pump (e.g., 200W panel, 12V pump) can lift water from 20 m depth at 1000 litres/hour. Store water in a 5000-litre plastic tank on a 2 m high stand to provide gravity pressure. Piping: use 25 mm HDPE pipes buried 30 cm deep to prevent sunlight damage. Troughs: concrete or plastic, 1 m long per 10 cows, with a float valve to maintain water level. Clean troughs weekly with a brush and chlorine solution (1 tablespoon per 20 litres). In dry areas, use a nose pump: cattle push a lever to drink, saving labour. For extensive grazing, a mobile trough on a trailer with a 1000-litre tank works. Always test water quality: if salty (above 3000 ppm total dissolved solids), cattle may refuse it. Add a shade over the trough to keep water cool. In cold highlands, prevent freezing by using black pipes and a trough heater. For calves, provide shallow troughs (15 cm deep) to prevent drowning. If using a river, fence off a drinking area with stones to reduce mud and contamination. Store a spare pump and pipes on farm. Train one person to check water flow daily and record usage. A reliable water system is the backbone of any cattle operation.

lessons.title: Waste Management Systems
lessons.body: A mature cow produces 15â20 kg of manure per day, plus urine. Poor waste management causes flies, odours, and disease. The simplest system is a daily scrape: use a rubber scraper or hoe to move manure from the shed to a concrete pad or pit. For a 20-cow herd, a manure pit 3 m x 3 m x 1 m holds about 3 months of waste. Cover the pit with a roof to prevent rain leaching nitrogen. Alternatively, compost manure: layer 30 cm manure, 10 cm crop residues (maize stalks), and a sprinkle of wood ash; turn every 2 weeks. After 8 weeks, it becomes black gold for crops. For liquid waste, build a urine channel: a 20 cm wide, 10 cm deep concrete gutter behind the cows, sloping to a 200-litre drum. Dilute urine 1:5 with water and use as foliar fertiliser. In zero-grazing units, use a slurry tank: a 5000-litre underground tank receives wash water and urine; pump it to a biogas digester if you have 10+ cows. A fixed-dome biogas plant (6 mÂ³) produces 2â3 hours of cooking gas daily from 20 cows. For bedding, use sawdust, wood shavings, or chopped straw; add 5 kg per cow per day. Remove soiled bedding weekly. Never let manure pile up against wallsâit breeds flies and corrodes concrete. If selling manure, dry it in thin layers and bag in 50 kg sacks. In areas with ticks, compost kills tick eggs. Always wear gloves and boots when handling manure. A good waste system turns a problem into profit: manure for crops, urine for pest control (diluted), and biogas for cooking.

lessons.title: Environmental Control and Ventilation
lessons.body: Cattle are sensitive to heat and humidity. In hot African climates, the temperature-humidity index (THI) above 72 causes heat stress: reduced feed intake, lower milk yield, and infertility. To control environment, first maximize shade. A simple shade structure: 3 m high poles with a thatch or shade cloth roof (80% shade factor) giving 5 mÂ² per cow. Plant trees like neem or mango on the north and west sides. Second, ensure ventilation. In a closed barn, install a ridge vent (0.5 m wide) and side vents (1 m high, adjustable). Use a 0.5 m diameter exhaust fan for every 10 cows if natural ventilation is poor. In open sheds, orient the long axis perpendicular to prevailing winds. Third, manage moisture: concrete floors with 2% slope and gutters reduce humidity. Use ceiling insulation (e.g., sisal sacks) under iron roofs to reduce radiant heat. In cold highlands (e.g., Ethiopia), prevent drafts: close side walls with mud or plastic sheeting, but leave a 0.3 m gap at the top. For calves, provide deep bedding (30 cm straw) and a heat lamp (100W) in cold nights. Fourth, control flies: use fly traps (a bucket with rotting fish) or spray with 1% permethrin every 2 weeks. Fifth, reduce dust: sprinkle water on feed alleys. Monitor temperature with a simple thermometer: if above 30Â°C, increase ventilation and provide extra water. In feedlots, use sprinklers (10 minutes every hour) to cool cattle. Remember, good ventilation prevents pneumonia, especially in calves. A well-ventilated barn smells fresh, not ammonia. Check ammonia levels by smellâif your eyes water, ventilation is inadequate.

quiz.q: What is the recommended diameter for a thorn-bush kraal for 20 cattle?
quiz.explanation: A 10â15 m diameter circular kraal provides adequate space for 20 cattle.

quiz.q: Which material is best for a roof in hot climates to keep the barn cool?
quiz.explanation: Thatch provides better insulation than iron or plastic, reducing heat inside the barn.

quiz.q: How much resting space does a mature cow need in a loose barn?
quiz.explanation: A mature cow requires about 4â5 mÂ² of resting space for comfort and hygiene.

quiz.q: What is the recommended roof pitch for corrugated iron sheets?
quiz.explanation: A 15â20 degree pitch allows proper water runoff without using too much material.

quiz.q: Which orientation of a shed helps minimize sun on long walls in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: An east-west ridge orientation minimizes direct sunlight on the long sides of the shed.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an open ridge in a barn roof?
options: B) To allow hot air to escape
quiz.explanation: An open ridge acts as a vent, allowing hot air to rise and escape, improving ventilation.

quiz.q: How deep should wooden fence posts be buried?
quiz.explanation: Burying posts 0.6 m deep provides stability for a 2 m post.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for the top strand of barbed wire in a cattle fence?
quiz.explanation: The top strand at 120 cm prevents cattle from leaning over and escaping.

quiz.q: What is the ideal width for a cattle crush (race)?
quiz.explanation: A 0.7 m width allows cattle to pass single file without turning around.

quiz.q: What chemical is commonly used in a footbath to prevent foot rot?
quiz.explanation: A 5% copper sulphate solution is effective against foot rot bacteria.

quiz.q: How much water does a lactating cow need per day in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: A lactating cow can drink 60â80 litres per day in hot conditions to maintain milk production.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for a water tank stand to provide gravity pressure?
quiz.explanation: A 2 m high stand provides enough pressure for troughs without a pump.

quiz.q: How often should water troughs be cleaned?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning with chlorine solution prevents algae and disease.

quiz.q: What is a nose pump used for?
options: A) Pumping water from a borehole
B) Letting cattle pump their own water
quiz.explanation: A nose pump is operated by the cow pushing a lever, providing water on demand.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended total dissolved solids (TDS) in cattle water?
quiz.explanation: Above 3000 ppm TDS, cattle may refuse water or suffer health issues.

quiz.q: How much manure does a mature cow produce per day?
quiz.explanation: A mature cow produces about 15â20 kg of manure daily.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dimension for a manure pit for a 20-cow herd?
options: A) 1 m x 1 m x 1 m
B) 3 m x 3 m x 1 m
C) 5 m x 5 m x 2 m
D) 10 m x 10 m x 2 m
quiz.explanation: A 3 m x 3 m x 1 m pit holds about 3 months of manure from 20 cows.

quiz.q: What is the ideal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for composting manure?
quiz.explanation: A 30:1 C:N ratio is optimal for microbial decomposition in composting.

quiz.q: How much biogas can a 6 mÂ³ fixed-dome plant produce daily from 20 cows?
quiz.explanation: A 6 mÂ³ biogas plant yields enough gas for 2â3 hours of cooking daily.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dilution ratio for using cattle urine as foliar fertiliser?
quiz.explanation: Diluting urine 1:5 with water prevents leaf burn and provides nutrients.

quiz.q: At what temperature-humidity index (THI) do cattle begin to experience heat stress?
quiz.explanation: A THI above 72 indicates heat stress, reducing feed intake and milk yield.

quiz.q: What percentage of shade factor is recommended for shade cloth in cattle pens?
quiz.explanation: An 80% shade cloth blocks most sunlight while allowing air movement.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a ridge vent in a barn?
options: B) To allow hot air to escape
quiz.explanation: A ridge vent allows hot air to rise and exit, improving ventilation.

quiz.q: How often should you spray permethrin to control flies in a barn?
quiz.explanation: Spraying every 2 weeks breaks the fly life cycle and reduces populations.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to check if ventilation is adequate in a barn?
quiz.explanation: If ammonia smell is strong enough to make your eyes water, ventilation is insufficient.

quiz.q: In cold highlands, what should you do to prevent drafts in a barn?
options: B) Close side walls but leave a top gap
quiz.explanation: Closing side walls with a top gap prevents cold drafts while allowing some ventilation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth of bedding for calves in cold weather?
quiz.explanation: A 30 cm layer of straw provides insulation and comfort for calves.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a footbath at the entrance of a cattle handling area?
quiz.explanation: A footbath with copper sulphate disinfects hooves and prevents foot rot.

quiz.q: How often should you check fences for damage?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks catch loose wires and rotten posts before cattle escape.

quiz.q: What is the ideal width for a loading ramp for cattle?
quiz.explanation: A 1.2 m wide ramp allows cattle to walk up single file without turning.

quiz.q: What is the recommended slope for a concrete floor in a cattle shed?
quiz.explanation: A 2â3% slope allows proper drainage without being too steep for cattle.
